section.title: Warning examples
section.p: Series tests are not recipes to apply by reflex. Each test has hypotheses, and those hypotheses are part of the mathematics.
This section collects the main warnings before we leave numerical series.
section.md: \text{A series test used without its hypotheses is not a test.}

statement.p: The harmonic series is the permanent counterexample to treating a_k\to 0 as a convergence test. In your own words, why is the term test only a one-way implication, and what mistake does that warning keep you from making?

hint.p: Necessary is not sufficient. The term test can prove divergence when terms stay large; it cannot prove convergence when they become small.

exercise.title: Why can the Ratio Test stay silent on both sides?

statement.p: The Ratio Test can return L=1 for a divergent series and also for a convergent one. In your own words, why is no information a genuine third conclusion rather than a failure to compute, and what should replace the Ratio Test in that case?

hint.p: A limit of 1 means the terms are not eventually geometric. Comparison, the Integral Test, or a p-series argument is then the right tool.

exercise.title: Why is a series test without its hypotheses not a test?

statement.p: The Integral Test needs a continuous, positive, decreasing function. The Alternating Series Test needs decreasing term sizes tending to zero. In your own words, why are those hypotheses part of the mathematics rather than extra paperwork?

hint.p: Each proof uses the hypotheses as a mechanism: rectangles sit above or below a curve, or bounces shrink. If the mechanism is missing, the conclusion is unearned.

subsection.p: The point is not to memorize a list of traps. The point is to keep the meaning visible.
A series is an accumulated limit:
Every test is a way to control that limit.
In the next chapter, the terms of the series will contain a variable:

Then an infinite sum becomes a function. That is where series stop being only numbers and become a new way to represent e^x, \sin x, \cos x, and many functions whose antiderivatives cannot be written in elementary form.

exercise.title: What are all series tests really controlling?

statement.p: Every series is a limit of partial sums. In your own words, why is every convergence test a way to control that limit, and how does that viewpoint keep the checklist from becoming a list of disconnected tricks?

hint.p: Comparison bounds running totals, the Integral Test compares them with area, alternating tests trap them in a shrinking gap, and ratio or root tests compare them with geometric tails. The object is always S_n.
